```{r setup}
library(onestepcox)
```

## The estimator

`onestepcox` provides closed-form estimators of the hazard ratio of a
two-group comparison of survival data that approximate the Cox partial
likelihood estimator. The main estimator of the package, called MH-Halley,
starts from the Mantel-Haenszel estimate of the log hazard ratio and takes
one Halley step on the Cox score equation. With `eta0` the Mantel-Haenszel
estimate and `U`, `I`, `J`, and `L` the score and its negative first,
second, and third derivatives at `eta0`, the estimate and its standard error
are

```
d    = 2 U I / (2 I^2 + U J)
eta1 = eta0 + d
se   = (I + J d + L d^2 / 2)^(-1/2)
```

The anchor is in closed form and the step is taken once, so no iteration is
needed, and `U`, `I`, `J`, and `L` are computed in the same pass over the
risk sets. Under proportional hazards, the Mantel-Haenszel and Cox estimators
are both root-n consistent for the log hazard ratio, so they differ by a term
of order `n^(-1/2)` in probability. The error of a Halley step is of the third
order in the error of its starting value, so the MH-Halley estimate differs
from the Cox estimate by a term of order `n^(-3/2)` in probability.

## Estimating the hazard ratio

`EstHR()` takes a formula and a data frame, as `survival::coxph()` does, or
vectors of times, event indicators, and group labels. The argument `method`
selects one or more estimators. The example below uses the German Breast
Cancer Study Group data in the `survival` package and compares hormonal
therapy with no hormonal therapy (variable `hormon`).

```{r estimate}
est <- EstHR(Surv(rfstime, status) ~ hormon, data = survival::gbsg,
             method = c("MH_Halley", "MH", "Pike", "Peto", "Cox", "Cox_NR"))
est
```

The treatment group has `hormon` equal to
`r attr(est, "groups")[["treatment"]]` (hormonal therapy), and the control
group has `hormon` equal to `r attr(est, "groups")[["control"]]`: without
the argument `control`, the control group is the smallest value of the group
variable.

`"Cox"` is the estimate of `survival::coxph()` with a tight convergence
tolerance, and `"Cox_NR"` is the Cox estimate computed by Newton-Raphson
iteration on the same risk-set summaries as the closed-form estimators,
until the Newton step is negligible. The MH-Halley estimate of the hazard
ratio is `r sprintf("%.4f", est["MH_Halley", "exp(coef)"])`, and the Cox
estimate (`"Cox_NR"`) is `r sprintf("%.4f", est["Cox_NR", "exp(coef)"])`.
Their log hazard ratios differ by
`r signif(abs(est["MH_Halley", "coef"] - est["Cox_NR", "coef"]), 2)`, and
the Mantel-Haenszel estimate, from which the step starts, differs from the
Cox estimate by
`r signif(abs(est["MH", "coef"] - est["Cox_NR", "coef"]), 2)`.

`plot()` draws the estimates and their confidence intervals as a forest
plot. It returns a `ggplot` object, which can be changed further with
`ggplot2`.

```{r forest, fig.alt = "Forest plot of the hazard ratios and their confidence intervals by method for the gbsg data."}
plot(est)
```

## Tied event times and strata

Tied event times are handled by the Efron method by default, as in
`survival::coxph()`, or by the Breslow method with `ties = "breslow"`.
Strata are given with `strata()` in the formula.

```{r strata}
EstHR(Surv(rfstime, status) ~ hormon + strata(grade), data = survival::gbsg,
      method = c("MH_Halley", "Cox_NR"), ties = "breslow")
```

All methods except `"Cox"` use the same risk-set summaries, which
`RiskTable()` returns: for each distinct event time (within strata), the
numbers at risk in the treatment and control groups (`n_T`, `n_C`), the
number of events in the treatment group (`O_T`), and the total number of
events (`O`).

```{r risktable}
head(RiskTable(Surv(rfstime, status) ~ hormon, data = survival::gbsg))
```

## Comparing estimators in simulations

`GenSimData()` generates two-group trials with exponential survival times,
uniform accrual, and an analysis at a fixed number of events, optionally with
dropout, strata, and times rounded up to multiples of a time unit (which
produces ties). `CompareOC()` simulates the trials of one or more scenarios
with `GenSimData()`, applies `EstHR()` to each, and summarizes, for each
method, the deviation from a reference estimator and the bias, root mean
squared error, and coverage relative to the true hazard ratio. The example
below uses `"Cox_NR"` as the reference: it iterates to the root of the score
on the same risk-set summaries and does not call `survival::coxph()` for
every replicate.

```{r simulation}
scenarios <- data.frame(
  label    = c("HR 0.7", "HR 2"),
  n_T      = 100,
  n_C      = 100,
  hazard_C = log(2) / 18,
  HR       = c(0.7, 2),
  a        = 12,
  E        = 150
)
nsim <- 100
res <- CompareOC(scenarios,
                 methods = c("Cox_NR", "MH_Halley", "MH_Newton",
                             "Pike_Halley", "MH", "Pike", "Peto"),
                 nsim = nsim, seed = 1, reference = "Cox_NR")
res
```

The column `time` is the computing time per replicate in seconds, which
depends on the machine.

```{r deviation, fig.alt = "Deviation of each method from the Cox_NR estimate of the log hazard ratio in the simulated scenarios."}
plot(res, what = "deviation")
```

```{r deviation-max, include = FALSE}
dev_max <- function(m) {
  max(res$summary$dev_max[res$summary$method == m], na.rm = TRUE)
}
```

Over the `r nsim` replicates of each scenario, the largest absolute
difference between the MH-Halley and the `"Cox_NR"` estimates of the log
hazard ratio was `r signif(dev_max("MH_Halley"), 2)`, compared with
`r signif(dev_max("MH_Newton"), 2)` for one Newton step from the same anchor
and `r signif(dev_max("Pike_Halley"), 2)` for one Halley step from the Pike
estimate.

## Large-sample limits

A one-step correction converges to the Cox limit only if its anchor does.
`LimitHR()` computes the limits of the estimators as the sample size grows,
under the design of `GenSimData()`. Under proportional hazards, the
Mantel-Haenszel and Cox estimators converge to the true log hazard ratio, and
so do the corrections from the Mantel-Haenszel anchor. Unless the hazard
ratio is 1, the Pike and Peto estimators and the corrections from the Pike
anchor converge to other values. The example below uses the design of the
simulation above, with one more, larger hazard ratio.

```{r limits, fig.alt = "Absolute large-sample bias of the Pike and Peto estimators and of the corrections from the Pike anchor against the hazard ratio."}
lim <- LimitHR(HR = c(scenarios$HR, 10), hazard_C = log(2) / 18,
               n_T = 100, n_C = 100, a = 12, E = 150)
plot(lim)
```

```{r limits-bias, include = FALSE}
lim_df <- as.data.frame(lim)
hr_max <- max(lim_df$HR)
bias_at <- function(m, hr) {
  lim_df$bias[lim_df$method == m & abs(lim_df$HR - hr) < 1e-8]
}
mh_halley_max <- max(abs(lim_df$bias[lim_df$method == "MH_Halley"]))
```

With a hazard ratio of `r hr_max`, the limit of the Pike estimator of the
log hazard ratio differs from the true value by
`r signif(abs(bias_at("Pike", hr_max)), 2)`, and one Halley step from the
Pike estimate still leaves a difference of
`r signif(abs(bias_at("Pike_Halley", hr_max)), 2)`. The MH-Halley limit is
the true value up to rounding error: the largest absolute difference over
these hazard ratios is `r signif(mh_halley_max, 1)`.

## Reproduction, validation, and the scripts of the article

The package comes with scripts that check it against published results and
an independent Python implementation. `inst/reproduce/` reproduces published
results, and `inst/validation/` compares the estimators with the Python
implementation and `LimitHR()` with large-sample simulations. Each script
writes its checks with a status (PASS, EXPLAINED, FAIL, or INFO) to a
`results/` folder, and `inst/validation/summarize_validation.R` counts them.
The counts recorded when the scripts were last run
(`validation/results/summary.csv` in the installed package) are:

```{r validation}
summary_file <- system.file("validation", "results", "summary.csv",
                            package = "onestepcox", mustWork = TRUE)
knitr::kable(utils::read.csv(summary_file))
```

The scripts that produce the tables and figures of the article accompanying
the package are in `inst/scripts/` (main text) and `inst/sup_info/`
(Supporting Information). Their results are kept in the GitHub repository and
are not part of the package build. When the package is installed, the
folders of `inst/` are placed at the top level of the installed package:

```{r folders, eval = FALSE}
system.file("reproduce", package = "onestepcox")
system.file("validation", package = "onestepcox")
system.file("scripts", package = "onestepcox")
system.file("sup_info", package = "onestepcox")
```
